scriptLabs.title: Find failed sign-ins with KQL
scriptLabs.brief: Reading Entra sign-in logs is the core SC-300 troubleshooting skill. Write a KQL query that surfaces failed interactive sign-ins over the last 7 days, ranked by user.
scriptLabs.hint: ResultType 0 means success. Filter to non-zero, then summarize with count() grouped by UserPrincipalName, and order the result.
scriptLabs.solution:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType != 0
| summarize failures = count() by UserPrincipalName, ResultDescription
| order by failures desc

scenarios.title: Ransomware hits the workstation fleet
scenarios.context: EDR fires: a ransomware binary is encrypting files on three workstations and reaching for a network share. You are the defender on call.

options.text: Isolate the affected hosts from the network
options.why: Containment first: isolating hosts stops lateral movement and cuts the ransomware off from the share.

options.text: Start restoring from backup immediately
options.why: Restoring before containment lets the ransomware re-encrypt the restored data.

options.text: Email all users warning them not to click links
options.why: User comms help, but the active encryption must be contained first - minutes matter.

options.text: Disable the EDR to stop the alert noise
options.why: Never blind your own telemetry during an incident.

steps.prompt: Which control would have PREVENTED the binary from executing at all?

options.text: Application allowlisting (deny by default)
options.why: The unsigned ransomware binary was never on the approved list - allowlisting stops it at execution.

options.text: A longer password policy
options.why: Password policy does not stop an already-running binary from executing.

options.text: More firewall rules on the perimeter
options.why: The binary is already inside; perimeter rules do not govern local execution.

options.text: Annual security awareness training
options.why: Training reduces clicks but cannot substitute for an execution control.

steps.prompt: Long-term: how do you blunt this attack class against the file shares?

options.text: Restrict which applications may write to network shares
options.why: Storage control by application: the ransomware's encryption path dies at the policy boundary even if it executes.

options.text: Give every user local admin rights for faster recovery
options.why: More privilege means faster ransomware spread - the opposite of the tiered-administration lesson.

options.text: Move the shares to USB drives
options.why: USB is an exfiltration and malware-ingress path, not a safer home for shares.

options.text: Turn off EDR on the file server to improve performance
options.why: Removing telemetry from the highest-value target is never the answer.

scenarios.title: The SOC sees a Kerberos ticket storm
scenarios.context: Overnight, one service account requested Kerberos service tickets for dozens of SPNs. The pattern matches Kerberoasting reconnaissance.

steps.prompt: What technique is most likely underway?

options.text: Kerberoasting - cracking a service account password offline from requested tickets
options.why: A burst of TGS requests for many SPNs is the classic Kerberoasting signature.

options.text: SQL injection
options.why: SQL injection targets web inputs, not Kerberos ticket requests.

options.text: Phishing
options.why: Phishing targets users, not service-ticket traffic.

options.text: DDoS
options.why: Ticket requests are low-volume and targeted - this is credential theft, not flooding.

steps.prompt: What is the immediate mitigation for the targeted account?

options.text: Rotate the service account password to a long random value and move it to a managed service account
options.why: The cracked material is the account's password hash - rotation invalidates it; managed accounts rotate automatically going forward.

options.text: Disable Kerberos across the domain
options.why: Disabling Kerberos breaks authentication domain-wide - disproportionate and destructive.

options.text: Delete the service account with no replacement
options.why: The service still needs an identity; deletion without replacement breaks the application.

options.text: Ignore it - ticket requests are normal
options.why: Bulk TGS requests from one account are not normal; ignoring forfeits the detection.

steps.prompt: What long-term hardening reduces this attack class?

options.text: AES-only Kerberos, strong random service passwords, and honeypot service accounts with alerts
options.why: AES resists offline cracking better than RC4, long random passwords raise the cost, and honey accounts turn the next attempt into an alert.

options.text: Shorter password expiry for all users
options.why: Expiry churn on user passwords does not address service-account ticket abuse.

options.text: More VPN capacity
options.why: Network capacity is unrelated to Kerberos ticket abuse.

options.text: Allowing RC4 for compatibility
options.why: RC4 is the weak encryption the attacker wants - keep it disabled.

scenarios.title: Rolling out Conditional Access safely
scenarios.context: You must enforce MFA and compliant-device requirements across the org's Entra ID tenant without locking out the business on day one.

steps.prompt: What is the safe FIRST step before enforcing a new Conditional Access policy broadly?

options.text: Run the policy in report-only mode and review what would have been blocked
options.why: Report-only shows the blast radius before enforcement - the learning-mode discipline applied to identity.

options.text: Enforce immediately on all users including break-glass accounts
options.why: Immediate broad enforcement risks lockouts - including of the emergency accounts you need to recover.

options.text: Delete all existing policies first
options.why: Deleting existing protections to add new ones leaves gaps and destroys the audit trail.

options.text: Apply the policy only to IT admins
options.why: Attackers target all users; admin-only coverage leaves the phishing surface open.

steps.prompt: Legacy authentication bypasses MFA. How should the policy treat it?

options.text: Block legacy authentication protocols explicitly
options.why: Legacy protocols cannot do MFA - leaving them open nullifies the MFA requirement.

options.text: Allow legacy auth for convenience
options.why: Convenience here is an MFA bypass - the exact hole attackers use.

options.text: Ignore it; attackers do not use legacy protocols
options.why: Attackers actively target legacy auth precisely because it skips MFA.

options.text: Require SMS MFA for legacy protocols
options.why: Legacy protocols cannot perform MFA at all - the protocol, not the method, is the problem.

steps.prompt: How do you protect emergency (break-glass) access accounts?

options.text: Exclude them from Conditional Access policies, with alerts on any use
options.why: Break-glass accounts must work when policies misbehave - exclusion plus monitoring is the standard pattern.

options.text: Enforce the strictest MFA policy on them with no exceptions
options.why: If the MFA infrastructure fails, you lose your last recovery path.

options.text: Delete them; they are a risk
options.why: Without break-glass accounts, a policy misconfiguration becomes an unrecoverable lockout.

options.text: Share one break-glass password with the whole IT team
options.why: Shared credentials destroy accountability - each emergency account stays separate and monitored.

Tiered administration (0/1/2), LAPS unique local passwords, Credential Guard, phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2, Windows Hello).
Password hash sync, pass-through authentication, or federation. PIM for just-in-time privileged roles; access reviews to revoke the unjustified.
OSI: 7 layers. TCP/IP: 4 layers. Map each attack class to the layer where it lives before placing controls.
SHA-2 family for integrity; salt passwords (rainbow tables); file-integrity monitoring; MD5 is dead (collisions).
Symmetric: one shared key (bulk data). Asymmetric: public/private pair (key exchange, identity). PKI binds identities to keys via certificates.
Compare against the vendor's published digest before installing.
At rest: disk/volume encryption. In transit: TLS. In use: memory protections. Key management is the real work.
Learning mode (baseline) -> policy design -> approval workflows -> enforcement. Never enforce on day one.
Per app, restrict: app-to-app communication, file/registry access, network egress. Browsers, Office, scripting hosts first - that is where LOLBins live.
Living-off-the-land binaries (PowerShell et al.): legitimate tools weaponized without malware. Ringfencing contains them.
Just-in-time elevation: rights granted temporarily, then removed. USB/removable media: policy decides which devices, users, data.
Triage fast, contain with playbooks, run the post-incident learning loop - each incident becomes a control.

answerBank.q: Which NIST publication anchors the Zero Trust material?
answerBank.a: NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture - the seven tenets, the policy engine / policy administrator / PEP logical model, and continuous diagnostics.

answerBank.q: What does the SC-300 path cover?
answerBank.a: Entra ID identity lifecycle (joiner-mover-leaver, B2B, access packages), Zero Trust Conditional Access, authentication and authorization (MFA, passwordless, OAuth2/OIDC/SAML), hybrid identity, governance (PIM, access reviews), and troubleshooting with PowerShell and KQL.
